state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a situation where alternate angles are not equal? How could you test whether angles \( p \) and \( q \) are actually equal in this specific case?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess if the lines aren't parallel, then the alternate angles could be different. But how would I actually measure angles \( p \) and \( q \) to see if they're equal? Do I need a protractor or something?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track with considering non-parallel lines. To measure angles \( p \) and \( q \) in this case, think about how you can use the properties of angles formed by a transversal intersecting two lines. Can you recall any angle relationships that might help you determine if they are equal?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I remember something about corresponding angles and how they can be equal if the lines are parallel. So, if the lines aren't parallel, maybe I can't just assume alternate angles are equal. But I'm still a bit confused about how to figure out if \( p \) and \( q \) are equal without measuring them. What should I look for?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the misconception by prompting the student to consider when alternate angles are not equal (parallel vs non-parallel lines), maintains high cognitive demand through questioning, and the student shows clear progress from assuming all alternate angles are equal to recognizing the parallel line condition, though the teacher could have been more explicit about what to look for in the diagram.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student toward understanding the relationship between parallel lines and alternate angles, never directly stating the answer, though could have used a more explicit counterexample when the student initially assumed all angles are equal.
